Customer Churn Analysis — Part 1: Data Preparation¶

Project: Customer Churn Analysis for Advanced Telecommunications Solutions (ATS)

Notebook role: Data Engineer — Preprocessing and Feature Engineering

Author: Ruyu (Grace) Liu

Purpose of this notebook¶

This notebook covers the foundational data preparation stage of the project:

  1. Load and inspect the raw dataset
  2. Clean the data (missing values, duplicates, outliers)
  3. Explore the data (EDA)
  4. Encode categorical variables
  5. Scale/normalise numeric features
  6. Split into train/test sets
  7. Export processed datasets for downstream use

Downstream consumers of this notebook's output:

  • Part 2 — Clustering Analysis needs a scaled version of tenure and MonthlyCharges only.
  • Part 3 — Predictive Modeling (ANN) needs the full feature set, encoded and scaled, split into train/test sets.

Sprint / Task Mapping (Jira reference)¶

This notebook corresponds to Sprint 1 — Epic: Data Preparation, broken down into the following tasks:

Task Notebook Section(s)

2. Load Dataset¶

Loading a working copy of the raw dataset (Dataset_ATS_v2.csv). The original file is kept untouched in its source location — all loading, cleaning, and transformation steps below operate only on this copy, so the raw data can always be re-referenced if needed.

Note: The dataset contains 7,043 customer records across 10 columns, covering demographic information (gender, SeniorCitizen, Dependents), service usage (tenure, PhoneService, MultipleLines, InternetService, Contract, MonthlyCharges), and the target label Churn.

Data Dictionary¶

Feature Type Values Description
gender Categorical (binary) Female, Male Customer's gender
SeniorCitizen Numeric (binary, 0/1) 0 = No, 1 = Yes Whether the customer is a senior citizen
Dependents Categorical (binary) No, Yes Whether the customer has dependents (e.g. children, other family members)
tenure Numeric (continuous) 0–72 Number of months the customer has been with the company
PhoneService Categorical (binary) No, Yes Whether the customer subscribes to phone service
MultipleLines Categorical (binary) No, Yes Whether the customer has multiple phone lines
InternetService Categorical DSL, Fiber optic Type of internet service the customer subscribes to
Contract Categorical (3 classes) Month-to-month, One year, Two year Length/type of the customer's contract
MonthlyCharges Numeric (continuous) 18–119 Customer's monthly bill amount, in dollars
Churn Categorical (binary) — target variable No, Yes Whether the customer has churned (left the company)

Notes on this dataset:

  • There is no unique customer ID column — each row represents one customer record, identified only by its combination of feature values.
  • tenure and MonthlyCharges are the two features used for the Clustering Analysis (Part 2), as specified in the project brief.
  • Churn is the target label used for the Predictive Modeling (ANN) in Part 3, and is not used as a predictor feature.

4. Data Cleaning¶

4.1 Missing Values¶

pd.DataFrame({"missing_count": missing, "missing_%": missing_pct})

Finding: No missing values were found in any column.

Decision: No imputation or row deletion is required for this dataset. (For reference — had missing data been present, the general approach would depend on the proportion missing and the feature's importance: e.g. drop rows if missingness is minimal and random; impute with median/mode for numeric/categorical features if missingness is moderate; consider dropping the column entirely only if a large majority of values were missing and the feature wasn't critical.)

4.2 Duplicate Rows¶

Finding: 302 duplicate row patterns were found (541 rows in total, including both first occurrences and repeats) — see the full listing above.

Decision: These rows are kept, not dropped, for now.

This dataset has no unique customer ID column, so there is no way to confirm whether these are truly the same customer recorded twice, or different customers who happen to share identical values across all 10 fields. Since tenure and MonthlyCharges are the two features used directly in the Clustering Analysis (Part 2), removing these rows would directly affect the density of points K-Means uses to determine cluster centroids — a decision that shouldn't be made without more certainty.

Recommendation: This should be raised with the mentor via the PM, or checked against the Data Engineer training materials — the absence of a unique customer ID is unusual for a real-world dataset and worth confirming before deciding how to handle these rows.

In [6]:

4.3 Outlier Check — All Features¶

Extending beyond tenure and MonthlyCharges, every feature is checked here for data quality issues — invalid values, unexpected categories, or implausible outliers — before moving into deeper exploratory analysis in Section 5. This is a sanity-check pass, not the full EDA narrative (which follows later).

In [7]:
# Visualise tenure and MonthlyCharges with both a boxplot (to spot outliers)
# and a histogram (to see the overall shape of the distribution)

    axes[0, i].set_title(f"{col} — Boxplot")

    axes[1, i].set_title(f"{col} — Histogram")

plt.tight_layout()

In [8]:
# Quantify potential outliers using the IQR method:
# any value beyond 1.5x the interquartile range from Q1/Q3 is flagged
for col in ["tenure", "MonthlyCharges"]:
    Q1, Q3 = df[col].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    IQR = Q3 - Q1
    lower, upper = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR, Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
    outliers = df[(df[col] < lower) | (df[col] > upper)]
    print(f"{col}: IQR bounds = [{lower:.1f}, {upper:.1f}], outliers found = {len(outliers)}")

Finding:

  • No missing, malformed, or unexpected category values were found in any of the 8 categorical fields — each contains only its expected set of values (e.g. Contract has exactly 3 categories, all others are binary).
  • tenure shows two notable spikes: a large group at 0 (new customers) and another at 72 (the maximum observed value, likely long-tenured customers or a cap in the data collection window). Both are plausible, real patterns rather than data errors.
  • MonthlyCharges shows a spike around $18–20, consistent with customers on a low-cost base plan.
  • No IQR-based outliers were flagged in tenure or MonthlyCharges (see quantitative check above).

Decision: No rows are removed at this stage. All feature distributions appear valid and consistent with real-world telecom customer behaviour.

Finding: The dataset is moderately imbalanced — roughly a 3:1 split between customers who stayed (No) and those who churned (Yes). This is a normal pattern for churn datasets and is worth flagging for the Predictive Modeling notebook (Part 3), where class imbalance can affect model evaluation (e.g. accuracy alone can be misleading; precision/recall/F1 matter more).

This imbalance is also why the train/test split in Section 8 uses stratified sampling (stratify=y) — this ensures the ~73/27 Churn ratio observed here is preserved in both the training and test sets, rather than risking an uneven split where one set ends up with a noticeably different churn rate purely by chance.

5.2 Numeric Feature Distributions — tenure and MonthlyCharges¶

Note: The visualisations in this section revisit tenure, MonthlyCharges, and the categorical features already plotted in Section 4.3. The purpose here is different, though: Section 4.3 checked these distributions for data quality issues (outliers, unexpected categories, invalid values). This section instead explores the trends and patterns within each variable — what the distribution shape suggests about the customer base, and how it might relate to churn behaviour — as a foundation for the deeper analysis that follows in Sections 5.4 and 5.5.

In [12]:

Finding:

  • tenure shows a somewhat bimodal pattern — a large group of relatively new customers (low tenure) and another cluster of long-standing customers approaching 72 months. This hints that natural customer groupings may already exist in the data, which is a good early sign for the clustering work in Part 2.
  • MonthlyCharges is more spread out, with a rise around the lower end (customers on basic/no add-on plans) and a broader spread at higher charges (customers with more services).

Finding: Gender is evenly split. Most customers do not have dependents and are not senior citizens. The majority have phone service without multiple lines, DSL is somewhat more common than Fiber optic, and Month-to-month is by far the most common contract type — consistent with the expectation that shorter, more flexible contracts tend to correlate with higher churn risk.

5.4 tenure vs MonthlyCharges, Coloured by Churn¶

This view is particularly relevant to the Clustering Analysis in Part 2, since these are the two features that will define the clusters.

In [14]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
sns.scatterplot(
    data=df, x="tenure", y="MonthlyCharges", hue="Churn",
    alpha=0.5, palette={"Yes": "#C44E52", "No": "#4C72B0"}, ax=ax
)
ax.set_title("Tenure vs Monthly Charges, by Churn Status")
plt.show()

Finding: Churned customers (red) are visibly concentrated in the low-tenure, higher-charge region of the plot, while long-tenure customers (regardless of charge level) churn far less often. This is a strong early signal that tenure and monthly charges alone can meaningfully separate customer segments by churn risk — a good justification for using exactly these two features in the clustering work.

5.5 Correlation Between Numeric Features¶

In [15]:
numeric_df = df[["SeniorCitizen", "tenure", "MonthlyCharges"]]
corr = numeric_df.corr()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4))
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, cmap="coolwarm", center=0, ax=ax, fmt=".2f")
ax.set_title("Correlation Matrix — Numeric Features")
plt.show()

Finding: tenure and MonthlyCharges show a weak positive correlation — they capture largely independent information about a customer, which supports using both together as complementary clustering dimensions rather than one being redundant given the other.

🗂️ Jira Task — Sprint 1 (Epic: Data Preparation): Feature encoding (categorical variables)

6. Feature Encoding¶

Categorical variables need to be converted to numeric form before they can be used in modelling (particularly for the ANN in Part 3; the Clustering notebook in Part 2 only needs the numeric tenure/MonthlyCharges columns and does not require this encoded set).

Approach:

  • Binary categorical variables (gender, Dependents, PhoneService, MultipleLines, InternetService, Churn) → Label Encoding (0/1), since each has exactly two categories.
  • Multi-class variable (Contract, 3 categories) → One-Hot Encoding, to avoid implying a false ordinal relationship between contract types.
In [16]:
df_encoded = df.copy()

# Binary categorical columns
binary_cols = ["gender", "Dependents", "PhoneService", "MultipleLines", "InternetService", "Churn"]

label_encoders = {}
for col in binary_cols:
    le = LabelEncoder()
    df_encoded[col] = le.fit_transform(df_encoded[col])
    label_encoders[col] = dict(zip(le.classes_, le.transform(le.classes_)))

# Show the encoding mapping used for each binary column, for transparency
for col, mapping in label_encoders.items():
    print(f"{col}: {mapping}")

gender: {'Female': 0, 'Male': 1}
Dependents: {'No': 0, 'Yes': 1}
PhoneService: {'No': 0, 'Yes': 1}
MultipleLines: {'No': 0, 'Yes': 1}
InternetService: {'DSL': 0, 'Fiber optic': 1}
Churn: {'No': 0, 'Yes': 1}
In [17]:
# One-hot encode the multi-class Contract column
df_encoded = pd.get_dummies(df_encoded, columns=["Contract"], prefix="Contract")

# Convert the new one-hot columns to int (0/1) rather than bool, for consistency
contract_cols = [c for c in df_encoded.columns if c.startswith("Contract_")]
df_encoded[contract_cols] = df_encoded[contract_cols].astype(int)

🗂️ Jira Task — Sprint 1 (Epic: Data Preparation): Feature scaling / normalisation

7. Feature Scaling¶

Two scaled outputs are prepared here for the two different downstream needs:

  1. Clustering-ready features — tenure and MonthlyCharges only, scaled with StandardScaler. K-Means relies on Euclidean distance, so these two features (which are on very different scales — months vs. dollars) must be standardised, or MonthlyCharges will dominate the distance calculation.
  2. Full feature set for ANN — all encoded features scaled together, since neural networks generally train better and converge faster on standardised inputs.
In [18]:
# --- 1. Clustering-ready scaled features ---
cluster_features = df_encoded[["tenure", "MonthlyCharges"]].copy()

scaler_cluster = StandardScaler()
cluster_features_scaled = pd.DataFrame(
    scaler_cluster.fit_transform(cluster_features),
    columns=["tenure_scaled", "MonthlyCharges_scaled"]
)

cluster_features_scaled.describe()

Note: Two separate scalers are used deliberately — the clustering scaler is fitted only on tenure/MonthlyCharges (matching exactly what Part 2 needs), while the full-feature scaler is fitted across all predictor columns for Part 3. Keeping these separate avoids Part 2 unintentionally depending on columns it doesn't use.

🗂️ Jira Task — Sprint 1 (Epic: Data Preparation): Train/test split & export processed data

8. Train/Test Split¶

This split is prepared for the Predictive Modeling notebook (Part 3). A stratified split is used to preserve the ~73/27 Churn ratio observed in Section 5.1 across both sets, since the dataset is moderately imbalanced.

The Clustering Analysis in Part 2 does not use this split — clustering is typically performed on the full dataset, since it's an unsupervised, exploratory technique rather than one being evaluated on unseen data.

In [20]:
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_scaled, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=y
)

print(f"Train set: {X_train.shape[0]} rows")
print(f"Test set:  {X_test.shape[0]} rows")
print(f"\nChurn rate — train: {y_train.mean():.3f}, test: {y_test.mean():.3f}")

Train set: 5634 rows
Test set:  1409 rows

Churn rate — train: 0.265, test: 0.265

Finding: The stratified split preserves the churn ratio closely between train and test sets, so the test set will provide a representative evaluation of model performance in Part 3.

9. Export Processed Datasets¶

The following files are exported to ../data/processed/ for use in the next two notebooks:

File Contents Used by
clustering_features_scaled.csv row_id + scaled tenure and MonthlyCharges Part 2 — Clustering Analysis
full_encoded_cleaned.csv row_id + full cleaned & encoded dataset (unscaled), including Churn Shared reference for both DAs — used by Clustering (Part 2) for post-hoc cluster profiling using categorical fields (e.g. Contract, InternetService), and available for the Predictive Modeling DA as needed
ann_train.csv / ann_test.csv row_id + scaled, encoded, split feature sets with Churn target attached Part 3 — Predictive Modeling

Why row_id matters: Neither clustering_features_scaled.csv nor full_encoded_cleaned.csv contains a customer ID (the source dataset doesn't have one — see Section 4.2). Since the Clustering Analysis in Part 2 trains K-Means on clustering_features_scaled.csv alone, but interpreting the resulting clusters requires joining the resulting cluster labels back to the categorical fields in full_encoded_cleaned.csv, both files need a shared key to join on reliably.

row_id is simply the row's position in the cleaned dataset at export time (0-indexed), added explicitly to both files so this join is safe regardless of whether either file gets re-sorted, filtered, or reloaded out of order later. The same reasoning applies to ann_train.csv/ann_test.csv — train_test_split reorders rows, so row_id is exported there too, preserving a traceable link back to the original dataset.

In [21]:
import os
os.makedirs("../data/processed", exist_ok=True)

# --- 1. Clustering features (scaled), with row_id for safe joining later ---
cluster_features_scaled_out = cluster_features_scaled.copy()
cluster_features_scaled_out.insert(0, "row_id", df_encoded.index)
cluster_features_scaled_out.to_csv("../data/processed/clustering_features_scaled.csv", index=False)

# --- 2. Full cleaned + encoded dataset (unscaled), with row_id ---
full_encoded_out = df_encoded.copy()
full_encoded_out.insert(0, "row_id", df_encoded.index)
full_encoded_out.to_csv("../data/processed/full_encoded_cleaned.csv", index=False)

# --- 3. Train/test sets for ANN (scaled features + target), with row_id ---
# X_train/X_test retain their original pandas index from before the split,
# which is exported here explicitly as row_id for traceability
train_out = X_train.copy()
train_out.insert(0, "row_id", X_train.index)
train_out["Churn"] = y_train.values

test_out = X_test.copy()
test_out.insert(0, "row_id", X_test.index)
test_out["Churn"] = y_test.values

train_out.to_csv("../data/processed/ann_train.csv", index=False)
test_out.to_csv("../data/processed/ann_test.csv", index=False)

10. Summary¶

What this notebook did:

  • Loaded and inspected the raw dataset (7,043 rows × 10 columns)
  • Confirmed no missing values; found 302 duplicate row patterns (541 rows) but kept them, since the dataset has no customer ID to confirm whether they are true duplicates or distinct customers with matching profiles — flagged for the PM/mentor to confirm
  • Confirmed no outliers in tenure/MonthlyCharges, and no unexpected values across all other fields
  • Explored the target variable (Churn, ~26.5% churn rate) and key feature distributions
  • Found an early visual signal that churned customers cluster in the low-tenure/higher-charge region — a good justification for the clustering approach in Part 2
  • Encoded all categorical variables (label encoding for binary, one-hot for Contract) into a single shared dataset used by both DAs
  • Produced two purpose-built scaled feature sets: one for clustering (tenure/MonthlyCharges only), one for the ANN (full feature set)
  • Created a stratified train/test split for predictive modelling, preserving the churn ratio
  • Added a row_id column to all exported files, to allow cluster labels (Part 2) and any other downstream outputs to be safely joined back to the full dataset
  • Exported all processed files for use in Parts 2 and 3

Next steps:

  • Part 2 (Clustering Analysis) picks up from clustering_features_scaled.csv, and joins back to full_encoded_cleaned.csv via row_id for cluster interpretation and labelling
  • Part 3 (Predictive Modeling) picks up from ann_train.csv / ann_test.csv
